title: Psychiatry
tagline: Psychiatric assessment, mood, anxiety and psychotic disorders, substance use, and treatments within the law
summary: Mental disorders are common and disabling, and every doctor meets them. This course covers psychiatric assessment and the mental state examination; mood, anxiety and psychotic disorders; substance use; eating and personality disorders; self-harm and suicide prevention; psychiatry in childhood, around childbirth and in later life; and psychological, drug and physical treatments together with the law on detention and capacity.
overview: Psychiatry uses the same clinical method as the rest of medicine: a history, an examination, investigations, a diagnosis and a plan. What is different is the material. The examination is mostly of what a person says and does, and the history is mostly about thoughts, feelings, behaviour and relationships. This course teaches that method in plain terms, with fictional cases throughout.

It starts with assessment: the psychiatric history, the mental state examination, the search for physical causes, the formulation and the assessment of risk. The disorder chapters follow: depression and bipolar disorder; anxiety, obsessive–compulsive and trauma-related disorders; schizophrenia and other psychoses; alcohol, opioids and other substances; eating disorders and personality disorders; and self-harm and suicide prevention, written in line with safe-messaging guidance. A lifespan chapter covers children and young people, mental illness around childbirth, and older people. The final chapter covers psychological therapies, psychiatric drugs and physical treatments, and the mental health and mental capacity law of England and Wales.

The course follows current UK guidance, mainly from NICE, with ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR criteria, and dates statements that may change. Short calculations appear where they help: predictive values of screening questionnaires, numbers needed to treat, alcohol units, BMI and lithium steady state. The material is for education only and is not medical advice. Management always follows current local guidelines and the BNF.
outcomes: Take a psychiatric history, perform and record a mental state examination, and write a biopsychosocial formulation.
Recognise when a psychiatric presentation may have a physical cause, and choose appropriate investigations.
Describe the diagnostic features of depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety and related disorders, psychotic disorders, substance use disorders, eating disorders and personality disorders.
Interpret screening questionnaires using sensitivity, specificity and prevalence, and explain why risk scales cannot predict suicide in individuals.
Assess and support a person after self-harm, using psychosocial assessment and safety planning in line with NICE NG225.
Outline evidence-based psychological treatments and the main classes of psychiatric drugs, with their monitoring and key adverse effects, including lithium, clozapine and valproate.

Recognise and outline the initial management of psychiatric emergencies, including alcohol withdrawal, Wernicke encephalopathy, opioid overdose, postpartum psychosis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome.
Explain how presentation and management differ in children and young people, in pregnancy and after birth, and in older people.

Describe the main provisions of the Mental Health Act 1983, the changes made by the Mental Health Act 2025, and the principles of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, and choose between them in common situations.
Address the physical health of people with severe mental illness as a core part of their care.

history.title: Moral treatment
history.detail: Philippe Pinel is appointed to the Bicêtre hospital in Paris, where patients are released from chains; in England the Quaker William Tuke founds the York Retreat in 1796. Both replace confinement with humane care, occupation and a calm environment.

history.title: Kraepelin's two psychoses
history.detail: In the sixth edition of his textbook, Emil Kraepelin separates dementia praecox from manic-depressive insanity on the basis of course and outcome. Long-term observation becomes central to psychiatric diagnosis.

history.title: The name schizophrenia
history.detail: Eugen Bleuler introduces the term schizophrenia for a group of disorders marked by disturbed association of thought, affect and sense of self, and argues that deterioration is not inevitable.

history.title: Electroconvulsive therapy
history.detail: Ugo Cerletti and Lucio Bini in Rome induce a therapeutic seizure with an electrical current. With anaesthesia and muscle relaxation added later, ECT remains the most effective treatment for severe depression.

history.title: Lithium
history.detail: John Cade in Melbourne reports that lithium salts calm patients with mania. Mogens Schou's trials in Denmark later establish lithium as a long-term treatment for bipolar disorder, with blood-level monitoring because of its narrow therapeutic index.

history.title: Chlorpromazine
history.detail: After Henri Laborit notices the calming effect of chlorpromazine in surgical patients, Jean Delay and Pierre Deniker in Paris report its effect in psychosis. Antipsychotic drugs make community care possible, and their movement and metabolic side effects become lessons in their own right.

history.title: The first antidepressants
history.detail: Nathan Kline and colleagues report the mood-elevating effect of iproniazid, a tuberculosis drug, and Roland Kuhn reports the antidepressant effect of imipramine. These findings lead to the monoamine hypothesis and later to the SSRIs.

history.title: Cognitive therapy
history.detail: Aaron Beck publishes his account of depression as shaped by negative thinking about the self, the world and the future, and goes on to develop cognitive therapy, the basis of modern CBT.

history.title: Operational criteria
history.detail: DSM-III, led by Robert Spitzer, introduces explicit diagnostic criteria for each disorder, building on the Feighner criteria. Diagnoses become more reliable, which makes research and service planning possible.

history.title: Recovery and national standards
history.detail: England's National Service Framework for Mental Health sets national standards for mental health care, including suicide prevention. The recovery movement, articulated by William Anthony in 1993, shifts the aim of care towards living a meaningful life.

references.title: Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry
references.authors: Paul Harrison, Philip Cowen, Tom Burns and Mina Fazel
references.note: Seventh edition. A clear, well-referenced core textbook for medical students and trainees, covering assessment, the main disorders and their treatment.

references.title: New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry
references.authors: John R. Geddes, Nancy C. Andreasen and Guy M. Goodwin (editors)
references.note: Third edition. The large reference work, for deeper reading on aetiology, evidence and specialist topics.

references.title: Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry
references.note: Fourth edition. A pocket guide to clinical practice, useful on the ward and in the emergency department.

references.title: Sims' Symptoms in the Mind: Textbook of Descriptive Psychopathology
references.note: Sixth edition. The standard account of psychopathology: how to describe and distinguish delusions, hallucinations and other abnormal experiences.

references.title: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry
references.authors: David M. Taylor, Thomas R. E. Barnes and Allan H. Young
references.note: Fourteenth edition. Practical, evidence-based guidance on psychotropic prescribing, monitoring and switching; always used alongside the BNF.

references.title: Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements for ICD-11 Mental, Behavioural or Neurodevelopmental Disorders
references.note: The official ICD-11 diagnostic guidance for mental disorders, used for the definitions in this course.

references.title: Mental Health Act 1983: Code of Practice
references.note: Statutory guidance for England on applying the Mental Health Act 1983; to be revised as the Mental Health Act 2025 is brought into force.

references.title: NICE guidelines on mental health and behavioural conditions
references.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
references.note: Current guidance cited in this course, including NG222 (depression), CG185 (bipolar disorder), CG178 (psychosis), NG225 (self-harm), NG69 (eating disorders) and CG78 (borderline personality disorder). Check the website for updates.
